meaning: ten (10); also builds 11 to 99: 十二 = 12, 二十 = 20

senses.en: ten: 十个人 'ten people', 十点 'ten o'clock'
in larger numbers: 十五 = 15, 三十 = 30, 九十九 = 99

examples.en: My younger brother is ten now.
examples.analysis: 十 + 岁 'ten years old': an age needs no verb, so there is no 是. The 了 at the end marks a new situation: he has just turned ten, or has reached that age by now.

examples.en: Let's meet at ten.
examples.analysis: 十 + 点 'ten o'clock'. The time goes before the verb 见 'see (you)', and 吧 at the end turns the plan into a suggestion: 'let's'. Context tells you whether it's morning or evening.

examples.en: Ten kuai? Isn't that too expensive?
examples.analysis: 十 + 块 + 钱 'ten kuai': spoken Chinese counts money in 块 (元 is the written unit). 太贵了 'too expensive'; the 吧 softens it into 'surely that's too much?', a typical haggling tone.

meaning: building with several floors; floor, story (三楼 'third floor')

senses.en: a building of several floors: 教学楼 'classroom building'
floor, story, after a number: 三楼 'the third floor'

measure.note: 一栋楼 'a building' (座 zuò is also used); 层 céng counts floors: 十层楼 'a ten-story building'

examples.en: My home is on the third floor.
examples.analysis: Number + 楼 names a floor: 三楼 'third floor'. In mainland China the street-level floor is 一楼, as in American English. 在 + place gives the location; no word for 'on' is needed.

examples.en: Which floor are you on?
examples.analysis: 几 + 楼 asks 'which floor?': 几 stands where the number will go in the answer (我在五楼). The word order stays the same as in a statement; only the question word fills the gap.

examples.en: The buildings at our school are all new.
examples.analysis: Here 楼 is the building itself. Chinese nouns usually don't change for plural (only words for people can add 们, as in 朋友们), so 都 'all' makes clear it is several buildings. 我们学校的楼 'our school's buildings' is the subject.

hook: 木 'wood' on the left marks a wooden structure; 娄 (lóu) on the right gives the sound.

meaning: to remember; to get something firmly into memory

senses.en: to fix in memory so it stays: 记住我的名字 'remember my name'
as a firm command at the start of a sentence: 记住，… 'remember this: …' (boss, teacher or parent tone)

examples.en: Have you learned my name yet?
examples.analysis: 记住 is 记 'to remember, take in' + 住 'hold fast': a result verb meaning it has been fixed in memory. 了吗 asks whether that result has been reached, 'has it stuck yet?'. 我的名字 is moved to the front as the topic, very common in speech.

examples.zh: 对不起，我没记住你的名字。
examples.en: Sorry, I didn't manage to remember your name.
examples.analysis: 没 + 记住: the speaker heard the name, but it didn't stay in memory. 没 negates the result. Compare 忘了 'have forgotten', which implies you once knew it and lost it.

examples.en: Remember, work starts at eight tomorrow.
examples.analysis: 记住 on its own at the start is an order, 'remember this!', firm like a boss, teacher or parent; between equals 别忘了 'don't forget' is softer. What to remember follows as a full sentence. 明天八点 'tomorrow at eight' comes before the verb 上班 'start work'.

related.en: to remember (still have it in mind); 记住 is the act of fixing it

meaning: to wash (hands, clothes, dishes)

senses.en: to wash something: 洗手 'wash hands', 洗衣服 'do the laundry'
to wash oneself: 洗澡 'take a shower or bath'

examples.en: Wash your hands first, then eat!
examples.analysis: 洗 + 手 is verb + object: the thing washed follows 洗. 先…再… 'first…, then…' puts two actions in order. With no subject, it's an instruction, typically from a parent at the table.

examples.en: I've washed your clothes.
examples.analysis: The clothes come first as the topic, then 我洗了 'I washed (them)'. 了 after 洗 marks the job as done. 洗衣服 is the everyday phrase for doing laundry, by hand or by machine.

examples.en: This cup hasn't been washed properly.
examples.analysis: 洗 + 干净 'wash clean': the second word gives the result. 没 says the result 'clean' was not reached, so the cup is still dirty. A handy complaint when a cup at a restaurant looks dirty.

hook: 氵 on the left is 'water'; 先 (xiān) on the right gives the sound.

meaning: (to do) what: what someone is doing or plans to do; what for

senses.en: what (someone) is doing or will do: 你干什么呢？ 'what are you up to?' (said sharply, 你干什么！ means 'what do you think you're doing?!')
what for, after coming or going: 你去北京干什么？ 'what are you going to Beijing for?'

examples.en: What are you doing?
examples.analysis: 在 before the verb marks 'right now', and 呢 at the end makes the question chattier. 干什么 is casual; 做什么 asks the same in a more neutral tone.

examples.en: Nothing much. I'm watching TV at home.
examples.analysis: 没 + 干什么 'not doing anything (special)' is a common reply to 你干什么呢. After a negative, 什么 means 'anything', not 'what'. The real answer follows: 在家看电视.

examples.en: What are you doing tomorrow afternoon?
examples.analysis: No future marker is needed: 明天下午 sets the time and 干什么 asks the plan, like English 'what are you doing tomorrow?'. The time words go before the verb.

collocations.en: what are you going off to do?

related.en: what to do; more neutral in tone

meaning: patient; sick person

senses.en: a patient, in a hospital or clinic
a sick person at home: 家里有病人 'someone at home is ill'

measure.note: 一个病人; 位 (wèi) is more polite: 这位病人

examples.en: I'm going to the hospital to visit someone who's ill.
examples.analysis: 看 here means 'visit', so 看病人 is 'visit a sick person'. Don't confuse it with 看病 'see a doctor' (or, for a doctor, 'treat patients'). Said by a doctor, the same sentence means 'I'm going to the hospital to see patients.' 去 + place + 看 chains two actions: go there, then visit.

examples.zh: 请问，新病人在几号房间？
examples.en: Excuse me, which room is the new patient in?
examples.analysis: 请问 'may I ask' opens a polite question, here to a nurse or desk. 新病人 'the new patient' is the subject; 在 + 几号房间 'in room number what?' asks for the room number.

examples.en: The patient can't eat anything right now.
examples.analysis: 不能 'can't, mustn't' passes on a medical rule. 吃东西, literally 'eat things', is the everyday way to say 'eat (anything)'; it is broader than 吃饭 'have a meal'.

related.en: to see a doctor; (of a doctor) to treat patients

meaning: younger brother

senses.en: younger brother
小弟弟: a friendly way to address a little boy

measure.note: 一个弟弟; 两个弟弟 'two younger brothers'

examples.en: My younger brother is at university in Beijing.
examples.analysis: 我弟弟 'my younger brother': with close family, 的 is often dropped. 上大学 'attend university'; 在北京 comes before the verb to say where.

examples.en: Do you have a younger brother?
examples.analysis: 有 + 弟弟 + 吗 asks 'do you have…?'. Chinese names siblings by age: 哥哥 is an older brother, 弟弟 a younger one. The answer is 有 'yes' or 没有 'no'.

examples.en: My younger brother is taller than me.
examples.analysis: A 比 B + adjective: 'A is more … than B'. The adjective stays bare (高, not 很高). 弟弟 is A here: the younger brother has outgrown his older sibling.

meaning: to meet; to see each other (in person)

senses.en: to meet up, see each other: 我们见面吧 'let's meet'. It takes no object: 'meet him' is 跟他见面, not 见面他

examples.en: Where shall we meet?
examples.analysis: 在 + place goes before 见面: 'at where meet?'. 哪儿 sits where the answer will go (在门口见面). There's no 'shall' in Chinese; the context makes it a plan.

examples.zh: 明天下午三点见面，好吗？
examples.en: Let's meet at three tomorrow afternoon, OK?
examples.analysis: Time goes before the verb, biggest unit first: 明天 → 下午 → 三点 → 见面. 好吗 'OK?' on the end turns the plan into a polite suggestion.

examples.en: We haven't seen each other for a year.
examples.analysis: Length of time + 没 + verb + 了 = 'haven't … for (a year)'. The final 了 says this is the situation up to now. 见面 needs no object: it already means 'see each other'.

hook: 见 'see' + 面 'face': to see each other face to face.

meaning: to come to; to arrive at (a place)

senses.en: to come to, arrive at a place, which follows directly: 来到北京 (more written or storytelling than everyday speech, which often just says 来 + place, or 到)

examples.en: I've been in Beijing for three years.
examples.analysis: 来到 + place + length of time + 了: 'it's three years since I came to Beijing'. The final 了 counts up to now. In plain chat people usually say 我来北京三年了; 来到 sounds a little more like a story or a speech.

examples.zh: 你是什么时候来到中国的？
examples.en: When did you come to China?
examples.analysis: 是…的 frames a past event to ask about one detail, here the time. 来到 + place takes the destination directly, with no word for 'to'. A common small-talk question for foreigners; in casual talk 你是什么时候来中国的？ is even more common.

examples.zh: 下午我们来到一家小饭店。
examples.en: In the afternoon we came to a little restaurant.
examples.analysis: In telling a story, 来到 + place moves the scene: 'we came to…'. 家 is the measure word for restaurants and shops. 我们到了一家小饭店 would also work; 来到 sounds more like storytelling.

related.en: to arrive; plainer and more common in speech

meaning: a little while; a moment (how long something lasts)

senses.en: (for) a short while, after a verb: 等一会儿 'wait a moment'

examples.en: Could you wait for me a moment?
examples.analysis: The person comes right after 等, then the length of time: 等 + 我 + 一会儿. 能…吗 'can you…?' makes it a polite request.

examples.en: Let's take a short break.
examples.analysis: Verb + 一会儿 = do it for a short time: 休息一会儿 'rest a bit'. 吧 at the end makes it a suggestion, 'let's'. English uses a noun ('a break'); Chinese keeps the verb.

examples.en: He sat for a little while and then left.
examples.analysis: Verb + 了 + 一会儿 'sat for a while': 了 goes between the verb and the length of time. 就走了 'then left': 就 shows the leaving followed soon after, so he didn't stay long.

collocations.en: sit for a while; stay a bit

related.en: adverb 'in a moment, soon': 我一会儿就来
after a verb, 'briefly, a bit': 等一下儿 'hang on'

meaning: younger sister

senses.en: younger sister
小妹妹: a friendly way to address a little girl

examples.en: This is my younger sister. Her name is Xiaohong.
examples.analysis: 这是 + person introduces someone: 'this is…'. English often just says 'my sister'; Chinese specifies whether she is older (姐姐) or younger (妹妹). 叫 + name gives her name.

examples.en: How old is your younger sister?
examples.analysis: 多大了 asks someone's age, literally 'how big (by) now?'; 了 asks about the age reached so far, as in the answer 十岁了. For a small child, people often ask 几岁了 instead.

examples.en: My younger sister doesn't like eggs.
examples.analysis: 我妹妹 is the subject. 不喜欢吃 'doesn't like eating': Chinese often puts 吃 in when talking about liking a food. 鸡蛋 'eggs' has no plural form.

hook: 女 'woman' on the left; 未 (wèi) on the right gives a hint of the sound.

meaning: computer (desktop or laptop)

senses.en: computer, desktop or laptop

measure.note: 一台电脑; casual speech also says 一个电脑

examples.en: My computer's broken.
examples.analysis: 电脑 is the subject; 坏了 'has broken', with 了 marking the change from working to not working. The same 坏了 is used for phones and other machines.

examples.en: Go ahead and use my computer.
examples.analysis: 用 + 电脑 'use the computer'. 吧 makes it an offer, 'go ahead', softer than a bare command. 我的电脑 'my computer' keeps 的, as is usual with things you own; casual speech sometimes drops it (我电脑坏了).

examples.en: How much is this computer?
examples.analysis: 这个电脑 'this computer': 台 is the proper measure word, but 个 is common in casual speech. 多少钱 'how much money' is the standard price question.

meaning: conscientious, careful; serious, not joking

senses.en: conscientious, careful: 他工作很认真 'he takes his work seriously'
serious, meaning it: 我是认真的 'I mean it'
before a verb, 'carefully': 认真听 'listen carefully'

examples.en: He takes his work very seriously.
examples.analysis: 他 is the topic and 工作很认真 says how he goes about his work: careful, thorough, not sloppy. 认真 is an adjective, so it follows 很 with no 是.

examples.zh: 我是认真的，不是开玩笑。
examples.en: I'm serious. I'm not joking.
examples.analysis: 是 + 认真 + 的 states where you stand: 'I'm being serious'. 不是开玩笑 'it's not a joke' backs it up. The line for when someone thinks you're kidding.

examples.en: Listen carefully, and don't talk.
examples.analysis: 认真 before a verb says how to do it: 认真听 'listen with full attention'. Written Chinese often adds 地 (认真地听); speech often leaves it out. 别 + verb is 'don't'.

meaning: hot; (verb) to heat up, warm up (food)

senses.en: hot (weather, food, drinks, a person feeling hot): 今天很热
to heat up, warm up: 热饭 'heat up the food'

examples.en: It's so hot today!
examples.analysis: 太 + 热 + 了: in speech this often means 'so hot!' rather than literally 'too hot'. There is no word for 'it' or 'is': the weather adjective is the whole predicate.

examples.en: Is it hot outside?
examples.analysis: 热不热 asks 'hot or not?': adjective, 不, adjective again. It is a neutral yes/no question, the same in meaning as 热吗. 外边 'outside' is the topic.

examples.en: The food's gone cold. I'll heat it up for you.
examples.analysis: Here 热 is a verb, 'to heat up'. Doubling it, 热热, makes it a quick, casual action, 'warm it up a bit'. 给你 'for you' comes before the verb. 冷了 'has gone cold' gives the reason.

collocations.en: to heat up food; hot food

hook: The four dots at the bottom (灬) are a form of 火 'fire'.

meaning: to be short of, lack; poor, not good enough

senses.en: to be short (of), be missing: 还差一个人 'still one person short'
poor, not up to standard: 菜太差了 'the food is awful'
in telling time, 'to': 差五分十点 'five to ten'

examples.zh: 还差一个人，等一会儿吧。
examples.en: We're still one person short. Let's wait a bit.
examples.analysis: 差 + amount = 'short by': the missing thing, 一个人, follows 差 directly, with no word for 'of'. 还 'still' says the gap hasn't closed yet.

examples.en: How much are you still short? I'll give it to you.
examples.analysis: 还差 + 多少钱 'still short by how much money?': the amount missing follows 差, and 还 'still' asks about the gap that remains. No subject is needed when it's clear who is short. 我给你 offers to cover the gap.

examples.en: The food at this restaurant is awful.
examples.analysis: Here 差 is an adjective, 'poor, bad', judging quality: of food, service or someone's skills. 太差了 'really bad'. 家 is the measure word for the restaurant; 菜 means the dishes.

related.en: missing, short: 少一个人 'one person missing'

meaning: hungry; (verb) to go hungry

senses.en: hungry: 我饿了 'I'm hungry'
to go hungry, be left hungry: 饿了一天 'went hungry all day'

examples.en: I'm hungry. Let's go and eat.
examples.analysis: 饿 + 了 marks a change of state, 'I've become hungry', which is why 我饿了 is the standard way to say 'I'm hungry'. 去吃饭吧 suggests going to eat.

examples.en: I'm not hungry. You go ahead and eat.
examples.analysis: 不 + 饿 'not hungry': no 了 here, because this is a plain state, not a change. 你们吃吧 'you all eat' is a polite go-ahead, the line for declining food at the table.

examples.en: You must be hungry. Have a bread roll first.
examples.analysis: 饿了吧 'you must be hungry, right?': 吧 turns a guess into a question that expects 'yes'. No subject is needed when talking to the person in front of you. 先 'first' means before the proper meal.

related.en: to eat; to have a meal

hook: 饣 on the left is 'food'; 我 on the right was the sound element.

meaning: student; pupil (from primary school to university)

senses.en: student, pupil (school or university)

measure.note: 一个学生; 名 (míng) in formal counts

examples.en: Which school do you go to?
examples.analysis: 学校 + 的 + 学生 'a student of (the) school'; 哪个学校 'which school' fills the describer slot. The question word sits where the answer goes: 我是北京大学的学生.

examples.en: There are thirty students in their class.
examples.analysis: Place + 有 + number + measure + noun = 'there are thirty students in…'. 个 is the measure word for 学生. The noun stays the same for one student or thirty.

examples.zh: 我不是学生了，在医院工作。
examples.en: I'm not a student anymore. I work at a hospital.
examples.analysis: 不是 + noun + 了 = 'no longer…': the final 了 marks the change. Then 在医院工作 'work at a hospital', with the place before the verb.

meaning: afternoon; p.m. (to about 6; later hours are 晚上)

senses.en: afternoon, from after lunch until about 6 p.m.
p.m. before a clock time: 下午三点 '3 p.m.' (for 7 p.m. and later say 晚上七点)

examples.en: Are you free this afternoon?
examples.analysis: 下午 alone means 'this afternoon' when the day is clear. Time words can go before or after the subject (你下午有时间吗 works too). 有时间 'have time' means 'be free'.

examples.en: We have a meeting at 3 p.m.
examples.analysis: 下午 + 三点 = '3 p.m.': the bigger unit comes first, then the clock time, and both go before the verb 开会 'hold a meeting'.

examples.en: I won't be home this afternoon.
examples.analysis: 不 + 在家 'not at home'. Chinese verbs don't change for future time; 下午 sets the time, and context (said in the morning, say) makes it 'this afternoon'. As a habit, the same line means 'I'm not home in the afternoons.'

collocations.en: good afternoon (formal: staff, hosts, broadcasts; friends say 你好)

hook: 午 is 'noon': 上午 is before noon, 中午 around noon, 下午 after noon, the same build as English 'afternoon'.

meaning: movement; action (a motion of the body)

senses.en: a movement or motion of the body: 这个动作 'this move'
the way someone moves: 动作快 'quick in his movements'

examples.en: This move is hard.
examples.analysis: 动作 is a single movement of the body, in sport, dance or exercise. 这个动作 'this move' is the subject; 很难 'hard' follows directly, with no 是.

examples.en: Move a bit faster!
examples.analysis: 动作快 'quick in your movements', with 一点儿 'a bit' after the adjective: 'be a bit quicker'. A nudge to someone who is dawdling.

examples.zh: 医生，这个动作我能做吗？
examples.en: Doctor, can I do this movement?
examples.analysis: 这个动作 is moved to the front as the topic: 'this movement, can I do (it)?'. The usual verb for performing a movement is 做. A typical question to a doctor or physio about exercise.

meaning: slow; (before a verb) slowly

senses.en: slow: 我的手机很慢 'my phone is slow'
doubled before a verb, 'slowly, take your time': 慢慢吃

examples.en: Please speak a bit more slowly.
examples.analysis: Verb + 慢 + 一点儿 'do it a bit slower': 一点儿 after the adjective means 'a bit more'. A key line for learners when someone talks too fast.

examples.en: Take your time eating. I'll head off first.
examples.analysis: Doubled before a verb, 慢慢 means 'slowly, take your time': 慢慢吃 'enjoy your meal, no rush'. 我先走了 'I'm leaving first' is the polite way to leave before others.

examples.en: My phone is so slow.
examples.analysis: 慢 'slow' works for machines as well as people or traffic. 太…了 frames it as a complaint, 'so slow!'. The opposite is 快 'fast'.

collocations.en: take care (to a guest who is leaving)

hook: 忄 on the left is 'heart'; 曼 (màn) on the right gives the sound.
